title: Solomon's Palace and Temple Furnishings
overview: This chapter describes Solomon's grand royal buildings and then the bronze and gold objects made for the temple of the LORD in Jerusalem.

parts.label: Solomon's royal buildings (vv. 1-12)
parts.note: Solomon spent thirteen years on a palace complex with a great hall of cedar pillars (probably called the Forest of Lebanon for its many cedar columns), a throne room for judging cases, his own home, and a house for his Egyptian wife. Some readers see the temple's quicker seven years as putting God's house first, while others hear a quiet hint that Solomon spent more on himself.

parts.label: The craftsman and two pillars (vv. 13-22)
parts.note: Solomon hired a master bronze worker from Tyre, a coastal city famous for metalwork, whose mother was Israelite; translations spell his name Huram or Hiram. He cast two huge free-standing bronze pillars, each about eight metres tall, for the temple entrance, named Jakin (also spelled Jachin), probably meaning "he establishes," and Boaz, probably "in him is strength," though why they bore these names is not certain.

parts.label: The great bronze Sea (vv. 23-26)
parts.note: The "Sea" was an enormous round bronze basin holding a vast amount of water, which according to 2 Chronicles 4:6 the priests used for washing. It rested on twelve bronze bulls facing the four directions, which some interpreters connect with Israel's twelve tribes, though the text does not say so.

parts.label: Wheeled stands and basins (vv. 27-40)
parts.note: Ten bronze carts on wheels each carried a basin of water, which 2 Chronicles says was used to rinse the animal offerings. They were decorated with lions, bulls, palm trees and cherubim, winged guardian figures linked with God's presence.

parts.label: Summary of the bronze work (vv. 40-47)
parts.note: Everything the craftsman made was cast in clay molds in the Jordan valley, where the soil suited metal casting. There was so much bronze that no one weighed it, which stresses how lavish the project was.

parts.label: Gold furnishings and David's gifts (vv. 48-51)
parts.note: Inside stood objects of gold: an altar for burning incense, the table for the bread of the Presence (loaves kept set out before God), and ten lampstands. Solomon then stored the silver, gold and objects his father David had set aside, completing what David had hoped to do.

disagreement: Readers differ on whether placing Solomon's long, lavish palace project beside the temple is simple praise of his greatness or a subtle early warning about his priorities, which later chapters show going wrong.
think: What do the things people put the most time and money into reveal about what they value most?
